1002.title: Silver in a shell
1002.hook: the king has just declared himself free, and the sage answers by asking why he still wants money
1002.carry: wanting grows from forgetting the self
1002.howItsDone: Some readers of the Ashtavakra Gita take chapters two, three and four together: Janaka's declaration, the sage's testing questions, and Janaka's calm reply, as a model of how a teacher checks a student's realization.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, aho: Janaka's cry of wonder, and every wave is water: the self in everything. Every wave is water: the self in everything. Today, the teacher answers the cry.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `EVERY WAVE IS WATER.`

segments.voice: What does a good teacher do when a student announces, I've got it? A whole chapter of joy has just poured out of King Janaka: spotless, at peace, salutation to me. Another book might end right there, the student shining and the teacher nodding. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't. Chapter three opens with the sage leaning in, his tone almost dry. If you really know yourself as the one, imperishable Self, he asks, why are you still keen on piling up wealth? A question aimed straight at a king with a treasury, and at anyone who has made a big announcement about themselves.
screen: `I'VE GOT IT.` → `THE TEACHER LEANS IN.` → `THEN WHY STILL PILE UP WEALTH?`

segments.voice: Much of the third chapter is questions like that, in paraphrase. You know the Self as one and imperishable; why the hunger to get more? Then a picture. Someone on a beach sees a glint in a shell, takes the mother-of-pearl for silver, and a little greed wakes up. The greed is real. The silver isn't. In the same way, he says, wanting for the world rises out of not knowing the Self. That's one of the central teachings of Advaita, the non-dual school: the hunger to grab and hoard grows from forgetting what you are, the atman, already whole. Teachers call that forgetting avidya, not-knowing. Spotless and at peace are easy words to say. The test is whether the hand still closes around the silver. Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. He's asking whether the knowing has reached his habits yet, or only his mouth. In the next chapter Janaka answers, calmly: the one who knows the Self moves through the world as though it were a game, not weighed down by it. He shows the sage where he stands. A claim, a test, an answer. In this tradition, knowing the Self shows in the hand, not only in the mouth. Someone who knows they're already whole doesn't need the shell to be silver.
screen: `THE TEACHER ANSWERS WONDER WITH A TEST.` · `SILVER IN A SHELL.` · `AVIDYA: WANTING GROWS FROM NOT KNOWING THE SELF.` · `HAS IT REACHED THE HABITS, OR ONLY THE MOUTH?` · then, large: `A CLAIM, A TEST, AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been reaching for lately: a purchase, a bit of praise, a result. Without judging it, look the way the sage looks at Janaka: silver, or a glint in a shell? Notice where the wanting sits in the body, the chest, the jaw, the hands. Then try the old Advaita move: the wanting is seen, and I am the one who sees it. If you pray, offer the wanting to God just as it is; either way, let the hand open a little.
Shukti. Mother-of-pearl, the shell mistaken for silver. In the Ashtavakra Gita, the sage tests the king by asking why he still reaches, like someone taking a shell for silver.

segments.voice: Your line: wanting grows from forgetting the self. Silver, or a shell? The hand will tell you. Until tomorrow.

1003.title: The great idler
1003.hook: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all
1003.carry: drop the doer, not the work
1003.howItsDone: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita read its praise of idleness, with Bhagavad Gita 3.27 and 5.8, as the end of the ego's sense of being the doer rather than of outward work; some Hindus close an action or a puja by offering it, with words like Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukti and the sage's test: why does the king still reach for silver that's only a shell? Wanting grows from forgetting the self.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `WANTING GROWS FROM FORGETTING THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke. Deep in the book, the sage says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like. But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. A book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises a master of idleness.
screen: `BOOKS ABOUT LETTING GO.` → `FORGET IT ALL.` → `A MASTER OF IDLENESS.`

segments.voice: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. After the line about forgetting, the sage goes on. You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all that, where wanting goes quiet. Then something like a diagnosis: everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. Then a verse that can sound like a joke. Happy is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. Read straight, that's a blessing on the couch. Many teachers read it another way, because the verses around it are about one kind of effort: the strain of the one who thinks, I am the doer. The Bhagavad Gita names that strain plainly. Deluded by ahamkara, the ego, a person thinks, I am the doer. And the one who knows the truth, it says, thinks, while seeing, hearing, walking, even breathing, I do nothing at all. That's one of Hinduism's big teachings: the work goes on, and the ego's claim on it drops. So the great idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. The dishes still get washed; nobody inside is clenching about it. The forgetting is read the same way. The sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, one more thing for the ego to own. The book has pointed at freedom for pages; now even the pointing drops away.
screen: `FORGET IT ALL.` · `UNHAPPY BECAUSE OF STRIVING.` · `AHAMKARA: 'I AM THE DOER.'` · `'I DO NOTHING AT ALL,' WHILE THE WORK GOES ON.` · then, large: `DROP THE DOER, NOT THE WORK.`

segments.voice: For these minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness: don't manage the breath, don't follow a technique, don't try to remember anything. Let breathing, hearing and seeing happen, and notice they happen without anyone pushing them. If you catch yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. If you pray, close the way many Hindus close an action, offering it: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna.
Great idler, the one in whom the inner striving has stopped, because the ego's I am the doer has gone quiet. Today, the Ashtavakra Gita's hardest line: forget it all.

segments.voice: Your line: drop the doer, not the work. The dishes still get washed. Same time tomorrow.

1004.title: Where is bondage?
1004.hook: the last chapter is one small word asked over and over: where?
1004.tomorrow: Why did the breath get up to leave?
1004.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita ends with Janaka's chapter of questions beginning with kva, where; some students reread it slowly at the close of their study, asking each where for themselves.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great idler, in whom the ego's I am the doer goes quiet: drop the doer, not the work. Today, the last chapter.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `DROP THE DOER, NOT THE WORK.` · `TODAY: THE LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Kva. In Sanskrit it means where. It's a small word, the kind a child uses looking for a lost shoe. And the last chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita is built almost entirely out of it. Verse after verse, Janaka asks where. Not where is my kingdom, or where did I leave the keys. He asks where the things are that this path spends so long seeking. By the end, the word has asked about nearly everything, and the book simply stops.
screen: `KVA: WHERE.` → `VERSE AFTER VERSE.` → `THEN THE BOOK STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape of it, in paraphrase. Where are the elements, Janaka asks, where is the body, the senses, the mind, for me, spotless by nature? Where is scripture? Where is knowledge of the Self? Then the line that stops a reader short: where is bondage, and where is liberation? A verse later: where is the karma already begun, where is freedom while living? Janaka asked about freedom on the first page; the sage told him he was free if he took himself as free. Now, at the end, the student isn't celebrating his freedom. For what he is, even bound and free have nowhere to stand. That's why it's a where and not a no. He isn't saying scripture is wrong or liberation a myth. He looks for them in awareness itself, and finds nothing there that needs them. That's Advaita's teaching on moksha, liberation, at its starkest: freedom isn't a prize you win, because the Self was never bound. On this reading, the medicine has done its work, and the bottle can go back on the shelf. The whole book in a breath: a king asks how to be free, a sage says he already is, and the king's last word is where. It also closes this year's lineage track, three roads Hindus have long named. Karma, the road of action: the Gita's chapters on action, and a year of service designed. Bhakti, the road of devotion: the Gita Govinda, the Bhagavata's tenth book, kirtan. Jnana, the road of knowing: the Vivekachudamani and this book. Plenty of Hindu families walk more than one at once, a puja in the morning, work offered by day, a page of scripture at night. None is asked to stand in for the others.
screen: `WHERE IS THE BODY, THE MIND, SCRIPTURE?` · `WHERE IS BONDAGE? WHERE IS LIBERATION?` · `A WHERE, NOT A NO.` · `MOKSHA: THE SELF WAS NEVER BOUND.` · then, large: `KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.`

segments.voice: Borrow Janaka's small word and ask it gently, without hunting for answers. Where is the body? Where is the mind? Where is the one who is trying to be free? After each where, rest in the quiet the question leaves.

1005.title: The breath gets up to leave
1005.hook: in an Upanishad the body's powers argue over who holds it up, until the breath gets up to leave
1005.carry: prana is life, not just air
1005.tomorrow: Why does yoga put the breath fourth?
1005.howItsDone: Pranayama is traditionally learned from a teacher, and for those who keep the daily sandhya rite it is part of prayer itself; in many lineages a session begins sitting upright, with gentle breath awareness and slow exhalation before any breath retention, stopping at any dizziness or strain.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita ended on one word, kva, where: the self was never bound. And the lineage track closed: karma, bhakti, jnana. Today, a new stretch: practices, deeper.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA, COMPLETE.` · `THE SELF WAS NEVER BOUND.` · `NOW: PRACTICES, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: The powers of the body are having an argument. Speech says it holds the body up. The eye says no, it does. The ear, the mind, the elements themselves all make the same boast. It's a scene from the Prashna Upanishad, told by a teacher named Pippalada to a student who asked which powers keep a living being going. In the middle of the shouting, one power gives a single warning and stops arguing. The breath. Prana. Nobody believes it, so it simply gets up, as if to leave.
screen: `THE BODY'S POWERS ARGUE.` → `EACH ONE BOASTS.` → `THE BREATH GETS UP TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens next, in paraphrase. Prana, the chief power, has warned them: don't be fooled, I'm the one holding this body together. They don't believe it, so prana rises to go. As it rises, every other power is pulled up with it, helpless to stay. When it settles back down, they all settle, like bees that rise when the king bee rises and settle when it settles. Speech, mind, eye and ear turn to prana and praise it. That's one of the Upanishads' big teachings: prana isn't just air. It's the life-power itself, the one the senses and the mind ride on. In Sanskrit the same word means breath and life. That's why pranayama, working with prana by way of the breath, sits inside Hindu prayer and not only in yoga class: the traditional daily sandhya rite, for those who keep it, sets its prayers between rounds of pranayama. If everything rises and settles with the breath, then working with the breath works with the rest too: the restless mind, the racing heart. This week takes the practices in order, gentle ones before stronger ones. Two warnings belong at the start. Breath practice is done gently: nothing forced, nothing held until it hurts. If there's dizziness or strain, stop and breathe normally. And anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, talks to a doctor before trying the stronger practices. Just the king bee, rising and settling, and everything else going with it.
screen: `PRANA RISES; EVERYTHING RISES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.` · `PRANA: BREATH, AND LIFE ITSELF.` · `PRANAYAMA SITS INSIDE HINDU PRAYER.` · then, large: `GENTLY. NOTHING FORCED.`

segments.voice: Sit with the spine easy and watch the breath rise and settle without changing it, noticing what goes with it: the belly, the ribs, the shoulders, even the thoughts. After a while, let the out-breath become just a little slower than before, still easy. If you pray, you can let one slow Om ride the last out-breath, the way many Hindus begin their prayers. If anything strains, let it go back to normal.
Pranayama sequences: breath practices set in an order, working with prana, the life the other powers rise and settle with.

segments.voice: Your line: prana is life, not just air. When the breath settles, everything settles with it. Rest well.

1006.title: The eight limbs of yoga
1006.hook: a baby falls into a praying woman's cupped hands, and grows up to set the breath fourth in line
1006.carry: yoga begins with the yamas, not the breath
1006.howItsDone: Where pranayama is taught in Patanjali's frame, it rests on the yamas and niyamas and follows posture work; some schools open with a chant to Patanjali, settle into a steady seat, move through gentle breath practices in order, and finish by resting in stillness or meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Upanishad's breath that rose, and every other power rose with it. Prana is life, not just air.
screen: `THE BREATH THAT ROSE.` · `PRANA IS LIFE, NOT JUST AIR.`

segments.voice: There's a well-loved legend about how Patanjali arrived. A devout woman named Gonika had cupped water in her palms to offer to the sun, praying for a child, and a tiny figure fell into her hands. She called him Patanjali: pata, fallen, and anjali, cupped hands. Devotees say he was Adishesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. Some yoga schools still open class with a chant to him. And his Yoga Sutra lays out yoga as eight limbs, in order. Anyone looking for breathwork might be surprised. The breath is fourth.
screen: `FALLEN INTO CUPPED HANDS.` → `PATANJALI.` → `EIGHT LIMBS. THE BREATH IS FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the order, in paraphrase. First the yamas, restraints in how you treat others: non-harm, truth, not stealing, self-restraint, not grasping. Then the niyamas, observances in how you treat yourself: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study, surrender to God. Then the seat. Then pranayama. Then the senses drawn in, concentration, meditation, absorption. That order is one of the big teachings of Hindu yoga: it's a path to freedom, and it starts with how you treat people, before anyone counts a breath. Look closer at the seat: posture should be steady and easy, a way of sitting that can be held without fuss. Once it's in place comes pranayama: a pause, a breaking, in the flow of in-breath and out-breath. Through it, the sutras say, a covering over the inner light grows thin, and the mind becomes fit for concentration. Each step makes the next one possible. An honest, unharming life quiets the mind that sits down. A steady seat lets the breath settle. A settled breath lets the mind gather. Skip one and the next wobbles. Many Hindu teachers say this is why yoga isn't only exercise: a breath class that skips non-harm and truth has skipped the first two limbs. The sutra doesn't list breathing exercises one by one; later manuals do. What it gives is the frame, each limb laid on the last like stones in a path.
screen: `YAMAS, NIYAMAS, SEAT, BREATH…` · `HOW YOU TREAT PEOPLE COMES FIRST.` · `A STEADY SEAT, THEN THE BREATH.` · `EACH STEP MAKES THE NEXT POSSIBLE.` · then, large: `YOGA BEGINS WITH THE YAMAS.`

segments.voice: Before you sit, choose one yama to carry today, non-harm or truth, and say it to yourself once. Then shift until the sitting feels steady and easy; let each out-breath slow a little, noticing the small pause at the bottom of it, without holding. 1007.title: Breath as an offering
1007.hook: in the middle of a list of offerings, the Gita slips in the breath itself

1007.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama understand it, with Gita 4.29, as an offering in itself; yajna also goes on as the fire rite at weddings and home havans, and many families offer food to God before eating it as prasad.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali's eight limbs: the yamas and niyamas, the seat, then the breath. Yoga begins with the yamas, not the breath.
screen: `THE EIGHT LIMBS.` · `YOGA BEGINS WITH THE YAMAS.`

segments.voice: Two armies wait on the field of Kurukshetra, and in chapter four of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, driving Arjuna's chariot, is making a list. Some offer their sacrifice in fire. Some offer their wealth, some study, some strict vows. It reads like a tour of the ways a person can give something up. Then, tucked into the list, a line that sounds almost like a breathing class. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. No altar, no grain, no butter poured on flames. Just the breath, handed back and forth.
screen: `THE GITA MAKES A LIST.` → `FIRE, WEALTH, STUDY, VOWS.` → `AND THEN: THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The verse, chapter four, twenty-nine, in paraphrase: some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, checking the movement of both, devoted to the regulation of breath. That last phrase is pranayama, right there in the Sanskrit. To hear how bold that is, remember what yajna, sacrifice, meant: the Vedic fire rite, grain and ghee poured into Agni, the fire, with chanted verses. Hindus still do it, around a wedding's sacred fire or a havan for a new home. Krishna keeps the fire and widens it. Around this verse he lists offerings with no fire at all: study, vows, the senses held back. A few verses later he says sacrifice made of knowledge is greater than sacrifice made of things. So the breath on this list isn't a warm-up before the real offering. It is one. That's one of the Gita's big teachings: a whole life can be yajna, offered, not only the moments at the altar. Notice the shape, too. It's already a sequence, the simplest there is. Each half is an offering into the other. The out-breath isn't an ending; it's what the in-breath is given to. Commentators read the verse in different ways. Some take it as a technical note on the in-breath, the out-breath and the hold between. Others read it more widely, as one more inner offering in a chapter full of them. The text leaves room for both. What it does settle is that the breath belongs on the list.
screen: `IN-BREATH OFFERED INTO OUT-BREATH.` · `YAJNA: THE FIRE RITE, WIDENED.` · `STUDY, VOWS, THE BREATH ITSELF.` · then, large: `A WHOLE LIFE CAN BE OFFERED.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, change nothing; notice where the out-breath ends, and let the next in-breath receive what the last one let go. Then watch the two turning points, out becoming in and in becoming out, without lengthening or holding anything, and after a handful of rounds let the breath carry on by itself. If you pray, you can hold the Gita's picture lightly in mind: breath given into breath.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the Gita's picture of one: in-breath offered into out-breath, and back.

1008.title: The lion and the breath
1008.hook: a fish overhears Shiva teaching yoga, and the manual that follows says tame the breath like a lion
1008.carry: steady breath, steady mind, learned from a guru
1008.howItsDone: In hatha yoga lineages, practice is received from a guru, and some sessions open with a bow to Adinatha, Shiva; breath practices are learned in order, gentle ones first, with longer holds left until later and sometimes taught one to one by a teacher who watches the student.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita put the breath on its list of sacrifices, in-breath offered into out-breath: even breath can be yajna, an offering.
screen: `BREATH AS AN OFFERING.` · `YAJNA.`

segments.voice: There's a legend in the Nath yogis' tradition about how hatha yoga reached people. Shiva was teaching yoga to Parvati by the sea, and a great fish lay listening in the water; in many tellings, a child was inside it. Every word went in, and out came a master: Matsyendra, lord of the fish. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual for yogis, opens with a bow to Adinatha, the first lord, Shiva, and names Matsyendra among the masters who handed the practice down. Then, in chapter two, where it starts teaching breath, it brings in a lion, an elephant and a tiger.
screen: `SHIVA TEACHES; A FISH LISTENS.` → `MATSYENDRA.` → `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.`

segments.voice: Chapter two, verse fifteen, in paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is brought under control slowly, little by little, so the breath is brought under control. Otherwise, it harms the one who practices. The next verse adds that breath practice done properly helps, and done wrongly brings illness. The warning is about pace. A few verses earlier, the chapter gives the reason breath matters at all: when the breath moves unsteadily, the mind is unsteady; when the breath is still, the mind is still. That's the hatha tradition's big teaching: breath and mind move together, so steadying one steadies the other. And it's why the manual keeps naming its teachers. Hatha yoga comes down as a parampara, a line of gurus reaching back, in the tradition's own telling, to Shiva. A lion isn't tamed from a book, and the stronger practices, long holds especially, are traditionally learned one to one, with a guru watching. Teachers call the pace krama, going in order, though the verse doesn't use the word. This week has followed that line: the breath the others rise with, the limbs before the breath, breath offered into breath, and now the pace. It began with the Ashtavakra Gita, where the sage tells Janaka that practicing meditation is itself his bondage; the hatha manual is practice from start to finish. The tradition keeps both.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · `UNSTEADY BREATH, UNSTEADY MIND.` · `PARAMPARA: FROM SHIVA, GURU TO STUDENT.` · `LONG HOLDS, LEARNED WITH A GURU.` · then, large: `THE TRADITION KEEPS BOTH.`

segments.voice: If you pray, begin as the manual does, with a bow to the first teacher, or to your own. Start with a few breaths as they come, then a gentle count: in for four, out for four. When that's easy, stretch only the out-breath to five or six, and if the chest, throat or jaw strains, return to the even count; that return is part of the sequence, not a failure of it. Near the end, drop the counting and let the breath settle by itself.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the pace of that order: little by little, the way a lion is tamed, under a guru's eye.
